segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus left the temple and was going on his way when his disciples came up to point out to him the buildings of the temple.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you not see all these things? Truly I tell you, not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and the end of the age?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “See that no one leads you astray.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Messiah,’ and they will lead many astray.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You are going to hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must happen, but the end is not yet.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For nation will rise up against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But all these things are the beginning of the birth pains.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then they will hand you over to affliction and will kill you, and you will be hated by all the nations because of my name.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then many will fall away, and they will hand one another over and hate one another.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Many false prophets will rise up and lead many astray.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And because lawlessness will multiply, the love of most will grow cold.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed in the whole inhabited world as a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of through the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: then those in Judea must flee to the mountains.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The one on the housetop must not go down to take what is in his house,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the one in the field must not turn back to take his cloak.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For then there will be great affliction, such as has not happened from the beginning of the world until now, and never will happen again.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if those days had not been cut short, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the chosen those days will be cut short.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Messiah!’ or ‘Here!’ do not believe it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For false messiahs and false prophets will rise up and give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: See, I have told you beforehand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So if they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; or ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For just as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Wherever the carcass is, there the vultures will gather.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Immediately after the affliction of those days, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And he will send out his angels with a great trumpet, and they will gather his chosen from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Learn the parable from the fig tree: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, you know that summer is near.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you also, when you see all these things, know that he is near, at the very doors.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, this generation will certainly not pass away until all these things take place.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will certainly not pass away.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But about that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of the heavens, nor the Son, but only the Father.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For just as the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and they knew nothing until the flood came and swept them all away, so too will be the coming of the Son of Man.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then two men will be in the field: one will be taken and one left.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and one left.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So keep watch, because you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But know this: if the owner of the house had known in what watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have kept watch and would not have let his house be broken into.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason you also must be ready, because the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household to give them their food at the proper time?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blessed is that slave whom his master finds doing so when he comes.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if that wicked slave says in his heart, ‘My master is taking a long time,’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and begins to beat his fellow slaves, and eats and drinks with the drunkards,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and will cut him in two and assign him his place with the hypocrites. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

notes.note: The Greek word means both arrival and presence, and in the period it was a regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. A first-century reader would have heard that royal overtone. Matthew is the only Gospel to use the word, and it recurs in verses 27, 37 and 39.

The Greek word is a title meaning the anointed king Israel was expecting, and here pretenders claim it as a title. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader, whereas “Christ” is now heard as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction in the Gospels.

A single Greek word lies behind both “nations” and “Gentiles” in English Bibles; in the plural it often means the non-Jewish peoples. In verses 9 and 14 “all the nations” could also be heard as “all the Gentiles”. The worldwide scope of the passage favors “nations”, which is the usual rendering here.

This is the ordinary Greek verb for passing someone into another’s custody, and Matthew uses the same word for what Judas, the chief priests and Pilate do to Jesus. Most versions vary the English, with “deliver up” here and “betray” in verse 10, and “betray” is a fair inference from the context there. One rendering is kept so that the reader can see the repetition the Greek reader saw.

The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression bearing down on people, not a technical term. Many versions keep “tribulation”, especially “great tribulation” in verse 21, but many readers now hear that as the name of a specific end-time period, which is more than the word itself says. The same word is used in verses 21 and 29.

The Greek was an everyday word for a public announcement of good news, used also of royal and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term and the name of a kind of book, so “good news” is closer to what the first readers heard. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The phrase comes from the book of Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), where it describes a detestable thing set up in the temple that leaves it desecrated and deserted. Jewish readers associated it with the profanation of the temple under Antiochus IV in 167 BC; 1 Maccabees 1:54 uses the same phrase. What event Jesus points to is disputed: many connect it with the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, others with a still future event, others with both.

This may be Jesus’s own words, directing the reader of Daniel to grasp the prophecy, or an aside by the evangelist to the person reading the Gospel (often aloud to a congregation). Many translations mark it as an aside with parentheses. Because Matthew has just named Daniel, it is left here within Jesus’s speech, but the other reading is equally possible.

The Greek is the ordinary adjective for someone or something picked out, used in the Septuagint of Israel as the people God chose. “The elect” is the usual English rendering, but it has become a specialized theological term, whereas the first readers heard a plain word. The meaning is not in dispute.

The Greek word usually means eagle but was also applied to vultures, and birds gathering at a carcass suggests carrion-eaters. Older versions have “eagles”; most modern ones have “vultures”. The saying appears to be a proverb, and its point here is debated; some see an allusion to the eagle standards of the Roman legions, but that is uncertain.

The Greek has no expressed subject and can equally mean “it is near”, that is, the end or the coming just described. “At the doors” suggests a person arriving, and most translations choose “he”, but several give “it”.

The word normally means the people alive at one time, and that is how Matthew uses it elsewhere. Because this seems to place “all these things” within the lifetime of Jesus’s hearers, some have proposed “this race” or “this kind of people”, while others limit “all these things” to the events leading up to the fall of Jerusalem. The usage of the period supports the plain sense; the difficulty is one of interpretation, not of translation.

Many later manuscripts lack these words, and some older English versions accordingly omit them. The earliest and most important witnesses include them, and they are probably original; scribes are more likely to have removed a statement that the Son does not know than to have added it. The parallel in Mark 13:32 has the words without significant variation.

The Greek word means a slave, someone owned by a master, not a hired employee, and the first readers would have pictured a slave manager set over the other household slaves. Most English versions soften it to “servant”, though some use “slave”. The word for “master” throughout the parable is the same Greek word translated “Lord” in verse 42.

notes.traditional: cut him in pieces; cut him asunder
notes.note: The verb literally means to cut in two, a savage punishment known in the ancient world. Because the slave is afterward assigned a place with the hypocrites, some take it figuratively as “punish severely” or “cut him off”, but a figurative use is not clearly attested elsewhere. The literal rendering is kept; the parable shifts at this point from the story to the judgment it portrays.
